explanation: Chemical cycling refers to the pathways by which chemical elements circulate through an ecosystem, involving both biotic (living) and geological (nonliving) components, also known as biogeochemical cycles (e.g., water, carbon, phosphorus, and nitrogen cycles). Each cycle contains three main components: 1) Reservoirs, which are chemical sources unavailable to producers. 2) Exchange pools, from which organisms directly take chemicals. 3) Biotic communities, where chemicals move along food chains. Human activities frequently disrupt these cycles. Biogeochemical cycles fall into two main types: gaseous cycles, where the chemical element is drawn from and returned to the atmosphere, and sedimentary cycles, where the element is drawn from the soil by plant roots, moves through consumers, and is returned to the soil by decomposers.

questions.q: What is a reservoir in a biogeochemical cycle?
opts: A source of chemicals that is directly taken up by organisms
A chemical source that is unavailable to producers
The community of decomposers in the soil
The atmosphere where gaseous exchange takes place
questions.exp: The notes define a reservoir as a 'source unavailable to producers.'

questions.q: What is the difference between a gaseous cycle and a sedimentary cycle?
opts: Gaseous cycles only occur in the ocean, while sedimentary cycles only occur on land.
In a gaseous cycle, the chemical is drawn from and returned to the atmosphere; in a sedimentary cycle, it is drawn from the soil by roots and returned by decomposers.
Gaseous cycles do not involve biotic communities, while sedimentary cycles do.
Gaseous cycles are exclusively driven by human activities, whereas sedimentary cycles are natural.
